catalog_quote: It has been established earlier that stress in the dialects of Moksha is mainly located on the word-initial syllable. Alternation in the position of stress has been considered to be associated with the distribution of the high and low vowels: stress is located on a non-initial syllable that contains a (or ä) if there is a high vowel (i, u) in the initial syllable. No reliable explanation of the variation has been offered, except for the assumption that the location of word stress might depend on the relative intrinsic duration of the syllable nuclei. ... Data from the dialects have shown, however, that the position of stress in words that contain high and low vowels in initial and non-initial syllables, respectively, varies; for this reason, stress in Moksha, particularly in certain dialects, has been considered to be relatively free. ... sources.citation: Shikunova, Alexandra (2024). Quality-conditioned stress as length: glide epenthesis in Moksha. Radical: A Journal of Phonology 6: 30-71 (lingbuzz 007524).
sources.quote: 'Default stress is on the leftmost syllable, however, vowel quality affects stress placement (Kukhto 2018). Syllables can be divided into heavy (with /a, ɛ, e, o/) and light (with /u, i, ə/). The stress is borne by the leftmost heavy syllable, or, in words without heavy syllables, by the initial one.' sources.quote: Paasonen: Mokshan stress 'ordinarily occurs on the first syllable of the word, but in words that have the high vowels i and u in the first syllable and the low vowel a (or ä) in a subsequent syllable, it tends to shift to the syllable in which low a (or ä) occurs ... dialects vary in this respect and ... variation is observable in the speech of informants from the same location as well.' sources.quote: (Estonian) Literature: dynamic stress on the first syllable, but if the first syllable has high u, i or reduced ə and a later syllable has low a, ä, stress shifts to that syllable (Paasonen 1903, Ravila 1929, Itkonen 1946, Bubrikh 1951, Devaev 1975). In Central and SE dialects the shift is 'reeglina' (as a rule); in Kolopino/Gorodishche the i/u/ə initial syllable may stay stressed; several authors call Moksha stress relatively free, rhythm and morphology (ma-gerund vs ma-infinitive: kutsema· vs ku·tsemă) also cited. Mid-Vad: stress usually initial, may fall on a later low-vowel syllable (kərga
sources.note: Measures vowel duration as a stress correlate in the Mid-Vad dialect of Moksha (two speakers, mono- to trisyllabic words): stressed vowels are longer than unstressed.

sources.citation: Kenstowicz, Michael (1994). Sonority-driven stress. Rutgers Optimality Archive ROA-33 (ms., MIT; published 1997 as 'Quality-sensitive stress', Rivista di Linguistica 9.1). Section 2 'Mordwin'.
sources.quote: Mokshan syllabic nuclei divide into 'narrow' [i, u, ə] and 'broad' [e, o, ä, a]. 'Tsygankin and Debaev (1975:32-33) summarize the distribution of stress as follows: wide vowels attract the word stress; in words with all narrow vowels or all wide vowels the stress is located on the initial syllable' and in mixed words 'stress falls on the first (i.e. leftmost) broad vowel' (puvəndəms vs tušəndat, kel'askə, noldasak). This is the categorical statement behind StressTyp2's 'leftmost heavy, else initial'.
sources.locator: sec. 2 Mordwin, ex. (5)-(7) (scanned the text); rule attributed to Tsygankin & Debaev 1975: 32-33
